title: Open Checklist Completion Log
description: A record that a checklist was worked through: what was ticked, when, by whom, and against which exact version of which checklist. Separate from the checklist itself because a checklist is a document and a log is an event. Designed so that an honest log is easy to produce and a dishonest one is hard to produce accidentally.

id.description: Unique identifier for this log entry. A UUID or any collision-resistant string.

checklist.description: Exactly which checklist was used. The content hash is the point of this block: without it, a log says only that the pilot ticked something called 'Cessna 172N Preflight', which is not evidence of anything six months later.

content_hash.description: SHA-256 of the canonical serialization of the checklist file, excluding its verification block. Proves which version was in the pilot's hand.

verification_at_use.description: The checklist's verification state at the time it was used. Copied into the log because the corpus state can change afterwards, and what matters is what the pilot was relying on.

identifier.description: Certificate number, student id, or club member number. Free text; never validated by the project.

started.description: When the pilot began working the checklist. RFC 3339 with an explicit offset; a local time with no offset is not evidence of when anything happened.

outcome.description: How the session ended. 'abandoned' and 'aircraft_rejected' are first-class outcomes: a preflight that found a problem and stopped is the system working, and a log format that can only record success quietly pressures people to record success.

recording.description: How this log came to exist. The most important block for whether the log is worth anything, and the one most likely to be quietly wrong.

mode.description: live = each item was marked at the moment it was done, timestamps generated by the device. retrospective = entered after the fact from memory. mixed = some of each. A retrospective log is still useful as a record of intent, but it is not evidence about timing and must never be presented as if it were.

clock_source.description: Where timestamps came from. A device clock the user can set is not a trusted time source, and saying so is more honest than implying otherwise.

edited_after_completion.description: True if any entry was changed after the session finished. Set by tooling, never by the user, and never resettable to false.

entries.description: One record per checklist item the pilot interacted with. Items that are not tickable (notes, cautions, warnings) may appear with state 'acknowledged' but must never appear as 'completed', because they were never tasks.

item_id.description: The item's stable id where it has one. Preferred over item_index, which shifts if the checklist is edited.

item_text.description: The item text as shown to the pilot. Denormalised deliberately: a log that only holds indices becomes unreadable if the checklist file changes or disappears.

state.description: completed = done as written. skipped = deliberately not done. not_applicable = does not apply to this aircraft or flight. deferred = to be done later in the sequence. failed = attempted and the aircraft did not comply. acknowledged = an information item the pilot marked as read.

reason.description: Required for skipped and failed. An unexplained skip is the thing a reviewer, instructor, or investigator will ask about first, so the format asks at the time instead.

observed_value.description: What was actually read, where the item calls for a value. This is what turns a tick into a record: 'fuel checked' is an assertion, '18.5 gal' is an observation.

allOf.comment: A skip or a failure without a stated reason is the gap that makes a log useless in review.
A live log must timestamp every entry; that is what distinguishes it from a retrospective one.

discrepancies.description: Squawks found during the check. The operationally valuable output of a preflight, and the reason a log is worth keeping even when nobody ever audits it.

disposition.description: What the pilot did about it. 'flown_anyway' exists because it happens, and a format that cannot record it produces logs that are quietly false.

attestation.description: The pilot's statement about this log. Optional, and deliberately not a legal instrument: it records that a named person stands behind the record.

previous_log_hash.description: SHA-256 of the pilot's previous log, forming a hash chain. Makes a log series append-only in practice: removing or backdating one entry breaks every later link. Cheap to implement and the only mechanism here that resists after-the-fact tidying.

allOf.comment: A live recording claims device-generated timestamps, so the session must have a finish time once it is not in progress.
Recording discrepancies but claiming a clean completion is contradictory.
